learning.title: Assert the row you mean by id; assert order only when order is the property
learning.trigger: A test indexes a page or a list - `items[0]`, `rows[0]`, `page.items[0]` - to reach the row it cares about, or asserts a list of ids in the order it happened to write or seed them.
learning.symptom: The test passes, then fails on the next run with the same rows in the opposite order. Nothing changed between runs. It reads as flake and gets re-run until green, which is how a real ordering bug becomes invisible.
learning.cause: `items[0]` is a hidden claim about ordering. A read ordered by a timestamp has no temporal answer when the rows were written in a single transaction, previewed in a single call, or seeded in a loop - PostgreSQL's `now()` is the transaction's start, so those rows share an instant exactly, and the query's tie-break (typically `<timestamp> desc, id desc`) then decides by a UUID. The expectation came from write order; the read never promised write order.
learning.rule: Reach the row you mean by id (`items.find((item) => item.id === wanted)`) and assert what is true of that row. Assert a sequence only where the order IS the property under test, and then derive the expectation from the read's documented ordering rather than from the order the test created the rows.
learning.evidence: Bakery #69 / PR 540, `tests/integration/read-the-tickets-linked-to-one-task_test.ts`. Two defects of this class in one small case, found by running it, not by any static gate: (1) links written by three HTTP calls - `ticket_task_links.created_at` defaults to `now()`, so two of them shared an instant and `created_at desc, id desc` broke the tie with a UUID; first run 158 passed / 0 failed, second run 157 / 1 with the two task ids swapped. Fixed by deriving the expected order from the ids the 201s return. (2) the same mistake one level up - two tickets cached by ONE preview call share `created_at`, and `mine.items[0].id === second.id` held on one run and failed on the next. Fixed by finding the row by id, after which three consecutive runs were green. See also `now-is-the-transaction-start.xml`, which covers the link-level instance. (3) a second, independent harness hit the same class inside the same two hours: qa-qa's cross-check for PR 540 asserted which ticket the second page carried and was red for exactly this reason, so the rule is not one author's preference about their own assertion - two people writing different code against the same read walked into it, one of them deliberately not depending on the other's work.
